extracted.intended_audience: OSHA rulemaking commenters; occupational safety researchers; economists; employers and other stakeholders interested in the proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention rule
extracted.subtask_description: Appendix from OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard presenting the literature synthesis and the agency's methods and assumptions for estimating productivity (non-health) effects of heat and the estimated productivity impacts of rest-break policies. Intended to support notice-and-comment on the proposed rule's economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of productivity loss per 1°F heat index (HI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Productivity loss per 1 °F HI is estimated from observed productivity at a REF condition and a HOT condition (e.g., using output per hour or per day), with percent loss computed relative to REF and divided by the HI difference between HOT and REF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rice harvest study – REF productivity 92 bundles/hour, HOT 63.8 bundles/hour → percent productivity at HOT = 69% → rate of productivity loss = 1.00% per 1 °F HI. Use the first hour of work where specified (OSHA used first-hour data in the rice study).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of REF condition
rubrics_metrics.description: REF condition is 'loosely, the minimum temperature at which heat begins to cause productivity loss' and is allowed to differ across study Groups; the average HI at REF uses the midpoint where a range was specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA groups studies and computes an average HI at REF within each group. If REF exceeds a policy trigger, the productivity loss at that trigger may be treated as 0% (see other criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust productivity-loss estimates for differences in break durations
rubrics_metrics.description: When study subjects had different amounts/durations of rest breaks than those in the proposed rule, OSHA adjusts the observed productivity loss rate by the ratio of the percentage of the work shift spent in breaks between the two scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sugarcane cutters had 60 minutes of breaks over a 9-hour shift (study) vs. proposed rule requires 35 minutes over an 8-hour shift → multiply the study's per-degree productivity loss by 1.52 (ratio of percent of shift spent in breaks) to adjust to proposed rule conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume 0% productivity loss at initial heat trigger when REF > initial trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: If the REF condition identified in the data is higher than the initial heat trigger used in the proposed rule, OSHA assumes productivity loss at the initial trigger is 0%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: REF 85.5 °F HI > initial trigger (80 °F HI) → productivity loss at 80 °F HI assumed 0%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate percent productivity loss into equivalent lost minutes in an 8-hour shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert estimated percent productivity loss to minutes lost by applying the percentage to an 8-hour (480-minute) work shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 4.50% productivity loss → 0.045 * 480 = 21.6 minutes lost per 8-hour shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify pacing effects of rest-break policies as minutes per shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate labor productivity loss attributable to pacing (self‑paced slower work) and estimate how if-needed and scheduled rest breaks change pacing, presenting findings as equivalent minutes per 8-hour shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimates: at the initial trigger, if-needed breaks reduce pacing by 2.8 minutes per 8-hour shift; at the high trigger, scheduled + if-needed breaks reduce pacing by 32.2 minutes per shift compared to no breaks, and by 31.1 minutes compared to if-needed-only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate assumption e.1 — pooled per-degree loss with break-policy-specific REF
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate an employee's expected productivity loss from pacing given a temperature and break policy by taking the average REF observed in studies with that break policy and combining it with the average productivity loss per degree observed across all studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach pools the per-degree slope across studies while allowing REF (intercept) to vary by break policy group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate assumption e.2 — cap productivity gains from breaks by observed pacing losses
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume that expected productivity gains from taking rest breaks do not exceed the productivity losses observed when employees work at a slower pace and do not take rest breaks; estimate gains by differences in productivity losses due to pacing measured at the initial trigger where the rest-break policy activates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: if rest breaks produced net increases in productivity, employers would already provide them; this limits estimated gains to observed reductions in pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies that did not measure temperature conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies are excluded from productivity/pacing estimates if they do not actually measure temperature conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples: Hostler et al., 2016; O'Neill et al., 2013.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies that assumed outdoor (forecasted) conditions applied to indoor workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that applied outdoor/forecast weather conditions to indoor workers rather than measured environmental conditions at the worksite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples: Cai et al., 2018; Adhvaryu et al., 2020.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where temperature conditions did not vary
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies with no variation in temperature conditions across observations (cannot estimate effect of heat on productivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed examples: Schlader et al., 2011; Uchiyama et al., 2022; Schranner et al., 2017; Constable et al., 1994; Morrissey-Bassler et al., 2024.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies with temperature range entirely below the initial heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies whose temperature (HI/WBGT) ranges are entirely below the initial trigger used for the proposed policy because they do not inform productivity losses at trigger thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Van Cutsem et al., 2015 (HI 77 °F), Federspiel et al., 2004 (HI 78.8 °F), Niemelä et al., 2002 (HI 77.2 °F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies with temperature range entirely above the high heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies whose temperature ranges are entirely above the high heat trigger because they do not provide comparative REF/HOT contrasts near the trigger points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Meegahapola and Prabodanie, 2018 (REF HI 90.1 °F); Wyndham, 1969 (REF HI 97.5 °F); Ismail, 2009 (REF HI 92 °F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies when temperature data cannot be reproduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies for which researchers or reviewers cannot reproduce the reported temperature data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Masuda et al., 2021; Sett and Sahu, 2014.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude review studies lacking empirical productivity data
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude literature-review articles that do not present new empirical productivity data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many review studies were excluded (list provided in the appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude modeling studies lacking empirical productivity data
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude modeling or theoretical studies that do not include empirical worker-level productivity data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many modeling studies were excluded (list provided in the appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where the outcome was heat strain rather than productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that report physiological heat-strain outcomes (core temperature, etc.) instead of direct or proxy measures of productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Wyndham, 1965; Kalkowsky and Kampmann, 2006; Miller et al., 2011; Ioannou et al., 2021a; Kaltsatou et al., 2020.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where the outcome was physical activity or maximum work capacity (not productivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies reporting physical activity levels or maximum work capacity measures when those are not reported or appropriate proxies for productivity in the workplace context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mix et al., 2019; Maresh et al., 2014.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where the outcome was cognitive performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies focused on cognitive performance measures rather than economic/productivity outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fine and Kobrick, 1987; Mazlomi et al., 2017; Spector et al., 2018.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where the outcome was heat-related injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies reporting heat-related injury incidence rather than productivity measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Park et al., 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where the outcome was loss of labor supply (including missed work hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies reporting absenteeism, hours worked, or labor supply changes rather than productivity per hour measures when estimating pacing/productivity losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Neidell et al., 2021 (ATUS); Graff‑Zivin and Neidell, 2014 (ATUS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where the outcome was non‑working time (e.g., unplanned breaks, idle time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that measure non-working time rather than production per hour (these are distinct outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Flouris et al., 2020 (unplanned break time); Ioannou et al., 2021b; Yi and Chan, 2017 (non-productive time); Li et al., 2016 (idle time); Zhao et al., 2009 (heat tolerance time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where the outcome was payroll or income data
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that report payroll or income (firm-level/payroll data) rather than worker-level productivity measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Deryugina and Hsiang, 2014; Park, 2016; Heal and Park, 2013.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where the outcome was crop yields
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude agricultural production outcome studies that report crop yields (farm-level output) rather than worker-level productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Houser et al., 2014.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies reporting firm-level output without worker-level data
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that assess firm output but lack worker-level productivity measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cachon et al., 2012.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies where productivity losses were self-reported
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies relying on self-reported productivity (surveys, focus groups) rather than objective production measures, for pacing/productivity quantification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Krishnamurthy et al., 2017; Zander et al., 2015; Langkulsen et al., 2010; Fahed et al., 2018; Budhathoki and Zander, 2019; Singh et al., 2015; Pogačar et al., 2019; Morera et al., 2020; Wadsworth et al., 2019.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies that provide a single productivity estimate for a range of temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that report one aggregate productivity estimate over a broad temperature range (cannot identify per-degree or threshold effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sadiq et al., 2019; Hansson et al., 2024; Glaser et al., 2022; Prince et al., 2020; Wegman et al., 2018; Bodin et al., 2016.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies that provide a single productivity estimate for multiple worksites with different conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies that aggregate across multiple worksites with different environmental/working conditions into a single productivity estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stevens, 2017; Gun and Budd, 1995.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies with non-comparable productivity data (varying observation or total work time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies where productivity data are not comparable due to different observation methods or differing definitions of total work time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sawka et al., 2015; Nag et al., 2006; Morrison, 1969.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies that report productivity for firefighting tasks only
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies limited to firefighting tasks because such emergency tasks differ in pacing and self‑pacing incentives from routine work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Larsen et al., 2015; Sol et al., 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies that provided breaks but did not specify break type or duration/frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies where breaks are reported but not categorized as scheduled vs if‑needed or not described by duration/frequency, because break policy cannot be mapped to proposed rule scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mitchell et al., 2018; Quiller et al., 2017; Ciuha et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude studies that used work-time shifting instead of rest breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude studies where adaptation occurred by shifting work time (e.g., doing work at cooler hours) rather than taking rest breaks, because this is a different policy/practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Morabito et al., 2020.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of HOT and REF days using the 75th percentile of daily HI
rubrics_metrics.description: In at least one study (Dally et al.), OSHA identified the days with the highest and lowest HI based on the 75th percentile of each day's HI to represent the range of temperatures corresponding to extreme productivity values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method was used to derive REF = 88.3 °F HI and HOT = 102.6 °F HI for the Dally et al. sugarcane cutter data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of first-hour productivity measures where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When study data report productivity by hour, OSHA used the first hour's productivity metrics to estimate the productivity loss attributable to heat in at least one example (rice harvesters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice influences the estimated per-degree loss (first-hour productivity may differ from later hours due to fatigue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling choices: pooled per-degree vs group-specific slopes and linearity assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Three alternative estimation approaches: primary approach allows per-degree rate of loss to differ by Group; a secondary approach pools the per-degree rate (e.g., 0.71% per 1 °F) while REF varies by Group; tertiary approach would pool REF and let per-degree slope vary by Group. OSHA is also considering pooled regression and nonlinear specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes implications: pooling different parameters yields different cost estimates (e.g., tertiary approach could produce implausible productivity-related costs), and a nonlinear specification could account for accelerating losses at higher temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pooled regression as an alternative to study-by-study estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: A pooled regression could estimate a single relationship between temperature and productivity loss (not differing by break policy), with separate estimates for how each rest-break policy modifies productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach could address heterogeneity challenges and could relax linearity assumptions if specified accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats for applying exposure-response (work capacity) functions to productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure-response work-capacity functions may under- or overestimate actual productivity effects because: (a) heat may reduce productivity via mechanisms beyond work capacity (central fatigue, cognition); (b) lab-derived maximum efforts may not reflect self-pacing or incentive structures in real workplaces; (c) assumed physiological thresholds (e.g., fixed acceptable heart rate) may not apply to all workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA highlights these caveats when considering using Hothaps, PWC, or similar functions for macroeconomic impact estimation or translating lab findings to field conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of labor productivity (BLS standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Labor productivity is 'a measure of economic performance that compares the amount of goods and services produced (output) with the amount of labor hours worked to produce that output' and is a 'ratio of output to hours worked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in labor productivity reflect output changes not explained by changes in hours worked; use worker-level output/hour measures when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable proxies for labor productivity and types of exposure-response functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proxies include physical work capacity, physical activity, and self-perceived labor productivity. Exposure-response functions come in two groups: empirically-derived functions based on data and functions based on recommended work-rest ratios from guidelines (NIOSH, ACGIH, ISO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hothaps function (empirical), Foster et al. PWC function (empirical lab), and guideline-based models; consider the origin of the function and applicability to field conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in interpreting labor-supply evidence: need to disentangle supply vs demand
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA notes that studies reporting reductions in hours worked could reflect labor supply responses, labor demand changes, or both; interpretation requires methods to distinguish these mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested approaches include stratifying by business cycle, examining wage effects, and assessing incentive structures (piece-rate vs salaried), since incentive structures affect whether workers will reduce hours or self-pace.
